correctness.rationale: The BFGS update acts nontrivially only on span{s,Hs}. In that plane its determinant is q=s^T Hs and its trace is q+1+m^2/q, with m^2=s^T H^2s-q^2. The endpoint spectral inequality gives the sharp bound m^2<=(q-1)(kappa-q), attained by support on the extreme eigenspaces. The resulting normalized trace is maximized uniquely at q=3kappa/(kappa+2), and solving the two-eigenvalue trace/determinant relation yields the closed form Gamma(kappa). The strict comparison Gamma(kappa)>kappa follows from an exact positive factorization. The packaged checker independently replays the algebra and explicit witness.

originality.rationale: Conditioning and scaling of quasi-Newton updates are established topics, and those general facts are treated as prior work. The closest full conditioning paper inspected discusses least-change measures, sizing, and the possibility that low-rank updates become ill-conditioned; Powell's full two-dimensional analysis studies a complementary regime with identity true Hessian and a poor initial approximation. The inspected sources do not state the exact worst one-update condition number from identity initialization relative to a true Hessian of condition kappa, nor the strict inequality for every kappa>1.
residual_risks: Shanno's 1970 paper could not be fully retrieved in this run, so an equivalent one-update specialization there cannot be excluded.
Older self-scaling or condition-optimal quasi-Newton literature may encode the same extremal formula under scaled-eigenvalue notation.
The theorem fixes B_0 to the minimum-curvature scalar identity; other initialization scalings may have different and potentially larger worst-case laws.

value.rationale: BFGS is designed to learn curvature while preserving positive definiteness, and matrix conditioning directly affects stability of quasi-Newton search directions and shifted systems. The theorem gives a complete sharp first-update law showing that even an exact quadratic secant can make a perfectly conditioned initial model more ill-conditioned than the true Hessian at every nontrivial condition number, with quadratic worst-case growth. This gives a precise structural reason why scaling and conditioning safeguards can matter before asymptotic Hessian recovery.
